chmmc-2019-individual-01.title: Volume of a tetrahedron two ways
chmmc-2019-individual-01.body:
Put the vertex at the origin, so the midpoints are $(1,0,0),(0,1,0),(0,0,1)$. These and the origin form a tetrahedron with three mutually perpendicular edges of length $1$, so its volume is $\frac16$.

The face opposite the origin is an equilateral triangle of side $\sqrt2$, with area $\frac{\sqrt3}{4}\cdot 2=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$. If $h$ is the distance from the origin to its plane, then $\frac13\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\cdot h=\frac16$, so $h=\frac{1}{\sqrt3}=\frac{\sqrt3}{3}$.

**Answer: $\frac{\sqrt3}{3}$**

chmmc-2019-individual-01.title: Distance to the plane x+y+z=1
chmmc-2019-individual-01.body:
The plane through $(1,0,0),(0,1,0),(0,0,1)$ is $x+y+z=1$. The distance from the origin is $\frac{|0+0+0-1|}{\sqrt{1^2+1^2+1^2}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt3}=\frac{\sqrt3}{3}$.

**Answer: $\frac{\sqrt3}{3}$**

chmmc-2019-individual-02.title: Subtract equations
chmmc-2019-individual-02.body:
The first two equations read $H^2=MC+1$ and $11H^2=(10M+C)C+1=10MC+C^2+1$. Subtract $10$ times the first from the second:
$$H^2=C^2+1-10\quad\Rightarrow\quad C^2-H^2=9.$$
The digit solutions of $(C-H)(C+H)=9$ are $C-H=1,\ C+H=9$, giving $C=5,\ H=4$ (the case $C-H=C+H=3$ would need $H=0$, which makes $\overline{HHH}$ meaningless). Then $MC=H^2-1=15$ so $M=3$.

Check: $444\times4=1776=355\times5+1$. So $\overline{HMC}=435$.

**Answer: 435**

chmmc-2019-individual-02.title: Search by cases on H
chmmc-2019-individual-02.body:
The first equation says $H^2-1=MC$ with $M\ge1$ and $C$ digits. Trying $H=2,\dots,9$ gives $H^2-1=3,8,15,24,35,48,63,80$. The second equation $11H^2=(10M+C)C+1$ then pins down the digits, and only $H=4$ ($MC=15$, $M=3$, $C=5$) works: $176=35\cdot5+1$ and $1776=355\cdot 5+1$.

**Answer: 435**

chmmc-2019-individual-03.title: Parity of the coin count
chmmc-2019-individual-03.body:
Every turn changes the number of coins by exactly $1$, so the parity of the number of coins alternates every turn. The players also alternate, so the first player always faces the same parity as the starting number of coins, and the second player always faces the opposite parity.

To remove the last coin the mover must face exactly $1$ coin, an odd number. Since the game ends, someone does this, and it is the first player precisely when the starting number of coins is odd. The starting number is $1,2,3$ with equal probability, so the first player wins with probability $\frac23$.

**Answer: $\frac23$**

chmmc-2019-individual-04.title: Parallel lines from equal areas
chmmc-2019-individual-04.body:
Since $[BLUR]=[BLUE]$ and both quadrilaterals contain triangle $BLU$, we get $[BUR]=[BUE]$. Both triangles share the base $BU$, so $E$ and $R$ are at equal distances from line $BU$; hence $ER\parallel BU$.

Then $\angle UER=\angle BUE$ (alternate angles), and $\angle BUE=\angle BLE=45^\circ$ because $B,L,U,E$ are concyclic and both angles subtend chord $BE$. In triangle $EUR$ with $EU=UR$ the base angles are $\angle UER=\angle URE=45^\circ$, so $\angle RUE=90^\circ$.

**Answer: 90**

chmmc-2019-individual-05.title: Polar description of the sweep
chmmc-2019-individual-05.body:
The tracks are the upper semicircles of radius $\sqrt3$ and $2$ about the origin $O$. If the baton $PQ$ has $P$ on the inner track and $Q$ on the outer, then $OP^2+PQ^2=3+1=4=OQ^2$, so the baton is always tangent to the inner track at $P$, and if $P$ is at polar angle $\varphi$ then $Q$ is at polar angle $\varphi\pm30^\circ$.

The baton cannot switch between the two sides, so fix one (say $Q$ at $\varphi+30^\circ$). Both ends must stay on the semicircles, which forces $0^\circ\le\varphi\le150^\circ$.

A point of the baton at distance $\rho\in[\sqrt3,2]$ from $O$ has polar angle $\varphi+\arctan\frac{\sqrt{\rho^2-3}}{\sqrt3}$. As $\varphi$ runs through $150^\circ$, on each circle of radius $\rho$ the baton covers an arc of exactly $150^\circ=\frac{5\pi}{6}$. Hence the swept area is
$$\int_{\sqrt3}^{2}\frac{5\pi}{6}\,\rho\,d\rho=\frac{5\pi}{6}\cdot\frac{4-3}{2}=\frac{5\pi}{12}.$$

**Answer: $\frac{5\pi}{12}$**

chmmc-2019-individual-06.title: Pair each term with its complement
chmmc-2019-individual-06.body:
Since $3\cdot11\cdot13\cdot19=8151$, the residues $(3-a,11-b,13-c,19-d)$ correspond to $8151-f(a,b,c,d)$ (all residues are nonzero, so $f\ne0$). Also $(3-a)+(11-b)+(13-c)+(19-d)=46-23=23$, so the complementary tuple is in the sum too. Pairing terms gives
$$\sum f=\frac{N}{2}\cdot 8151,$$
where $N$ is the number of tuples with $a+b+c+d=23$.

Count $N$ by cases on $d$ (with $a\in\{1,2\}$, $1\le b\le10$, $1\le c\le12$):
- $11\le d\le18$: $-2d+41$ tuples each, total $19+17+\dots+5=96$;
- $d=9,10$: $20$ each, total $40$;
- $1\le d\le 8$: $2d+3$ each, total $5+7+\dots+19=96$.

So $N=232$ (confirmed by direct enumeration) and the sum is $116\cdot8151=945516$.

**Answer: 945516**

chmmc-2019-individual-07.title: Geometric series
chmmc-2019-individual-07.body:
Write $\cos n\theta=\frac{e^{in\theta}+e^{-in\theta}}2$ and sum two geometric series with ratios $\frac{e^{\pm i\theta}}3$:
$$\sum_{n\ge0}\frac{\cos n\theta}{3^n}=\frac12\left(\frac1{1-\frac{e^{i\theta}}3}+\frac1{1-\frac{e^{-i\theta}}3}\right)=\frac{1-\frac{\cos\theta}{3}}{1+\frac19-\frac{2\cos\theta}{3}}=\frac{9-3\cos\theta}{10-6\cos\theta}.$$
Setting this equal to $1$: $9-3\cos\theta=10-6\cos\theta$, so $\cos\theta=\frac13$.

**Answer: $\frac13$**

chmmc-2019-individual-08.title: Parametrize the solutions
chmmc-2019-individual-08.body:
Taking positive roots, $\frac{a+b}{2}=\frac{b+c}{2019}=t$. Then $2t$ and $2019t$ are integers, and since $\gcd(2,2019)=1$, $t=m$ is an integer. So $a=2m-b$ and $c=2019m-b$ for a positive integer $m$, and we need $1\le b\le 2m-1$ together with $a,c<N:=2019^2$.

- For $m\le2019$ every $b\in[1,2m-1]$ works, giving $2m-1$ choices. Total $\sum_{m=1}^{2019}(2m-1)=2019^2$.
- For $m>2019$ we need $2019(m-2019)<b\le 2m-1$. Only $m=2020$ ($b=2020,\dots,4039$: $2020$ values) and $m=2021$ ($b=4039,4040,4041$: $3$ values) leave a nonempty range; larger $m$ do not.

Total: $2019^2+2020+3=4076361+2023=4078384$ (confirmed by computer).

**Answer: 4078384**

chmmc-2019-individual-09.title: Track vertices 1 and 3
chmmc-2019-individual-09.body:
Let $p_k(v)$ be the probability of being at vertex $v$ after $k$ jumps. From any vertex the frog lands in $\{1,3\}$ with probability $\frac12$ for $k\ge1$ (from $1$ or $3$ via the diagonal, from $2$ or $4$ via the two adjacent jumps), so $p_k(1)+p_k(3)=\frac12$ for $k\ge1$ and $p_k(2)=p_k(4)=\frac14$.

The difference $d_k=p_k(1)-p_k(3)$ satisfies $d_{k+1}=-\frac12d_k$: the vertices $2,4$ feed $1$ and $3$ equally, while from $1$ the frog goes to $3$ w.p. $\frac12$ and from $3$ to $1$ w.p. $\frac12$. With $d_0=1$ we get $d_k=(-\frac12)^k$, so $p_{2018}(1)=\frac12\left(\frac12+2^{-2018}\right)=\frac14+2^{-2019}$.

The last two vertices have labels summing to $3$ exactly when they are $\{1,2\}$: the frog is at $1$ or $2$ after $2018$ jumps and then makes the adjacent jump to $2$ or $1$ (probability $\frac14$). The probability is
$$\frac14\big(p_{2018}(1)+p_{2018}(2)\big)=\frac14\left(\frac14+2^{-2019}+\frac14\right)=2^{-3}+2^{-2021}.$$
Hence $m+n=3+2021=2024$ (the exact fraction was confirmed by computer).

**Answer: 2024**

chmmc-2019-individual-10.title: Use phi^n + phi^(n+1) = phi^(n+2)
chmmc-2019-individual-10.body:
Since $\phi^2=\phi+1$, we may replace digits $011$ by $100$ and back. Starting from $1=1_\phi=0.11_\phi$:
$2=1.11_\phi=10.01_\phi$, $4=2+2=100.1111_\phi$, $6=1010.0001_\phi$, and $7=6+1=1011.0001_\phi=1100.0001_\phi=10000.0001_\phi$.

Check: $\phi^4+\phi^{-4}=L_4=7$ (a Lucas number). A representation with a single $1$ would make $7$ a power of $\phi$, which it is not, so two $1$s is the minimum.

**Answer: $10000.0001_\phi$**

chmmc-2019-individual-11.title: Median length and law of cosines
chmmc-2019-individual-11.body:
By the law of sines $a=BC=2R\sin60^\circ=\sqrt3$. The median from $A$ has length $m_a=\frac32AG=\frac{\sqrt6}{2}$, and $m_a^2=\frac{2b^2+2c^2-a^2}{4}$ gives $2b^2+2c^2=6+3=9$, i.e. $b^2+c^2=\frac92$.

The law of cosines gives $a^2=b^2+c^2-bc$, so $bc=\frac92-3=\frac32$.

Computing the area two ways, $\frac12bc\sin60^\circ=\frac12a\cdot AD$, so $AD=\frac{bc\sin60^\circ}{a}=\frac{\frac32\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}{2}}{\sqrt3}=\frac34$.

**Answer: $\frac34$**

chmmc-2019-individual-12.title: Reduce with the rules
chmmc-2019-individual-12.body:
From the first two rules, $f(1,2)=f(2,1)=0$. For $a\ne b$ the third rule and antisymmetry give $f(a+2b,b)=f(b,a+b)+b=-f(a+b,b)+b=-f(b,a)=f(a,b)$, so $f(a+2b,b)=f(a,b)$.

Let $b=2^i$ (even). Put $g(k)=f(1,k)$. Then $g(2)=0$, and for $k\ge3$, $g(k)=-f(k,1)=-(f(1,k-1)+1)=-g(k-1)-1$, so $g(k)=0$ for even $k$ and $-1$ for odd $k$.

- $b^2+1=1+2b\cdot\frac b2$, so $f(4^i+1,2^i)=f(1,b)=g(b)=0$.
- $b^2-1=(2b-1)+2b\left(\frac b2-1\right)$, so $f(4^i-1,2^i)=f(2b-1,b)=f(b,b-1)+b$. For $b\ge4$: $f(b,b-1)=f(b-1,1)+(b-1)=g(b-2)+1+(b-1)=b$ (as $b-2$ is even), so $f(4^i-1,2^i)=2b=2^{i+1}$. For $i=1$: $f(3,2)=f(2,1)+2=2$.

Hence the sum is $2+\sum_{i=2}^{2019}2^{i+1}=2+(2^{2021}-8)=2^{2021}-6$. A direct computer evaluation of the recursion for small cutoffs agrees with $2^{N+2}-6$.

**Answer: $2^{2021}-6$**

chmmc-2019-individual-13.title: Count the possible total heights
chmmc-2019-individual-13.body:
A new tower of height $h$ is attached by a wall of length $h$, so it adds $9h+3h=12h$ to the cost. The cost is $9\cdot2^n+12S$, where $S$ is the total height of all towers other than the central one, so we count the possible values of $S$. The central tower must have at least one wall (a lone tower is connected to nothing), so $S\ge1$.

Let $M_k$ be the maximum total height of a non-central tower of height $2^k$ together with everything below it (it has $3$ free directions): $M_0=1$ and $M_k=2^k+3M_{k-1}$, so $M_k=3^{k+1}-2^{k+1}$. The central tower has $4$ directions, so $S_{\max}=4M_{n-1}=4(3^n-2^n)$.

- Small values: $S<2^n$ forces a single child of height $2^{n-1}$ followed by a chain, giving the $n$ values $2^n-2^j$ for $j=0,\dots,n-1$.
- Large values: each tower has three or four sub-branches of half the size, which gives enough freedom that every integer $S$ with $2^n\le S\le S_{\max}$ is attainable (checked by exhaustive computation for $n\le6$).

So the number of values is $n+\big(4(3^n-2^n)-2^n+1\big)=4\cdot3^n-5\cdot2^n+n+1$. For $n=1,\dots,6$ this is $4,19,72,249,818,2603$, matching exhaustive enumeration. For $n=1000$ it is $4\cdot3^{1000}-5\cdot2^{1000}+1001$.

(The official answer $4\cdot3^{1000}-5\cdot2^{1000}+1002$ additionally counts the lone central tower, which breaks the connectivity rule.)

**Answer: $4\cdot3^{1000}-5\cdot2^{1000}+1001$**

chmmc-2019-individual-14.title: Count with roots of unity
chmmc-2019-individual-14.body:
Since $n\equiv-1\pmod{n+1}$, the number $(\overline{a_1\dots a_n})_n\equiv\sum_i(-1)^{n-i}a_i$. Let $\omega=e^{2\pi i/(n+1)}$. For $t=1,\dots,n$: $\sum_{a=0}^{n-1}\omega^{ta}=\frac{1-\omega^{tn}}{1-\omega^t}=-\omega^{-t}$ and $\sum_{a=0}^{n-1}\omega^{-ta}=-\omega^{t}$.

The number of $n$-tuples (with $a_1\ge0$) whose alternating sum is $\equiv0$ is $\frac1{n+1}\big(n^n+\sum_{t=1}^n\Pi_t\big)$, where $\Pi_t$ has $\lceil n/2\rceil$ factors $-\omega^{-t}$ and $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ factors $-\omega^{t}$.
- $n$ even: $\Pi_t=1$, so the count is $\frac{n^n+n}{n+1}$.
- $n$ odd: $\Pi_t=-\omega^{-t}$ and $\sum_{t=1}^n(-\omega^{-t})=1$, so the count is $\frac{n^n+1}{n+1}$.

Tuples with $a_1=0$ are the same problem with $n-1$ digits (the last digit keeps sign $+$), giving $\frac{n^{n-1}+1}{n+1}$ for $n$ even and $\frac{n^{n-1}+n}{n+1}$ for $n$ odd. Subtracting,
$$|S_n|=\frac{n^n-n^{n-1}+n-1}{n+1}\ (n\text{ even}),\qquad |S_n|=\frac{n^n-n^{n-1}-n+1}{n+1}\ (n\text{ odd}),$$
which agrees with brute force for $n\le 11$.

Now reduce mod $n$ (note $n+1\equiv1$ and $n^{n-1}\equiv0$): $|S_n|\equiv-1$ for $n$ even and $|S_n|\equiv1$ for $n$ odd. So:
- $n$ even: $n\mid2019-1=2018=2\cdot1009$, so $n=2$ or $2018$.
- $n$ odd, $n>1$: $n\mid2020=2^2\cdot5\cdot101$, so $n=5,101,505$.

**Answer: $2,5,101,505,2018$**

chmmc-2019-individual-15.title: Tower of Hanoi
chmmc-2019-individual-15.body:
The non-leading terms are the $2019$ degrees $0,\dots,2018$. Think of degree $d$ as a disk of size $d$ and its coefficient in $\{-1,0,1\}$ as the peg it sits on. A swap moves disk $n$ from peg $a$ to peg $b$ only if no smaller disk is on peg $a$ or peg $b$, which is exactly the Tower of Hanoi move rule. So $\mathcal P$ is the set of Hanoi positions with $2019$ disks, and $\mathcal B$ is the three positions with all disks on one peg.

The state graph of Hanoi with $N$ disks is the Sierpinski graph, whose three corners are the elements of $\mathcal B$. We want the positions whose largest distance to the three corners is as small as possible: that minimum is $s$ and the number of positions attaining it is $p$. For $N$ disks, $s=3\cdot2^{N-2}$ and $p=6$ (verified by breadth-first search for $N\le 9$: $s=6,12,24,48,\dots$ and exactly $6$ positions for $N\ge3$).

With $N=2019$: $s=3\cdot2^{2017}$, $p=6$, so $p\cdot s=18\cdot2^{2017}=2^{2018}\cdot3^2$.

**Answer: $2^{2018}\cdot3^{2}$**
